the N-terminal region (amino acids 1-160) of ER is not required for synergism with upstream activating proteins and that the N-terminal deletion mutant exhibits enhanced affinity for the estrogen response element.
a deletion of the N-terminal transactivation domain in the estrogen receptor increases synergism with upstream transcription factors and enhances binding to the estrogen receptor element.

the deletion of the N-terminal 159 residues of the ER results in a protein with reduced basal activity and enhanced synergism with upstream transcription factors and binding to the estrogen-response element (ERE).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the AF1 domain of the estrogen receptor in transcriptional synergism and in binding to the estrogen receptor element.
the role of the internal transactivation domain (AF1) in transcription activation by XER.
the role of the internal N-terminus of the ER in transcriptional activation and in DNA interaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a deletion in the N-terminal region (amino acids 1-160) of the estrogen receptor leads to an enhanced affinity of the receptor for the estrogen response element and to increased synergy with upstream activator proteins.
the N-terminal region is important for the transcriptional activity of ER, but it is dispensable for the interaction with the ERE.

the N-terminal deletion mutant, XER160-586, has a reduced basal activity, but enhanced affinity for the estrogen response element (ERE), and exhibits a greater degree of synergism with upstream activating factors than wild type XER.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the N-terminal domain of the estrogen receptor is important in both transcriptional activation and binding of the receptor to its cognate DNA element, but that it is dispensable for the synergistic interaction of estrogen receptor with other transcription factors bound at upstream elements.

the N-terminal region (AF1) of ER contains two separable functions, an activation function which can be compensated for by an upstream activator, and an interaction function which is required for optimal DNA binding.

the N-terminal region is required for full transactivation by ER and is important for the interaction of ER and its DNA response element, but that an N-terminal region is not required for synergism by ER and other transcriptional activator proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the N-terminal region is important for both transactivation and DNA binding.
the N-terminal region is required for optimal transcriptional activation by XER, but that the N-terminal deletion mutant can still exhibit significant synergism with other transcription factors.

the N-terminal region (amino acids 1-586) of XER is not required for transcriptional synergism with an upstream activator or for DNA binding, but it is required for maximal basal activity on an ERE-containing promoter.
